source.version_note: Scientific Reports 15:34706, published 6 October 2025. Supplied file includes main article only, not the supplementary materials or OSF datasets. PDF creation/modification metadata postdate first publication; no change history is inferred.
source.verification_method: All seventeen supplied pages read, including seven tables, complete dilemmas, methods and references. All six figures visually inspected at PDF pages 3, 5, 7, 9, 10 and 11. Crossref verifies article identity/date. Simple partial-eta/F/p reconciliation checks use printed values; no supplement, preregistration or raw-data reanalysis is claimed.

citation.title: The power of justifications to repair human-robot trust, even under moral disagreement

reading.source_scope_note: Three short online narrative experiments measuring human blame and perceived robot/human trustworthiness. No live robot, actual consequential choice, behavioral reliance or verified machine ethical capacity. Analyses exclude respondents rejecting robots as proper blame targets; trust outcomes are expectations of trustworthiness, not a directly measured vulnerability state.
access_limits: Full supplied main article and all main figures/tables read. Extensive SM contains detailed exclusions, all message wording, factor analyses and robustness tests and was not supplied/read here.

OSF preregistrations/data links are documented but not opened or reproduced. Books, earlier papers and the cited 2023 preprint remain secondary; no independent replication is inferred from citation alone.

study.samples: US-registered Prolific adults not in prior related studies. Reported experiment datasets N=471, 1,088 and 2,037, totaling 3,596, ages 18–93. These headline Ns are not the final available-case N for each analysis: exclusions of robot-disqualifying responses and Does-not-fit missing trust ratings reduce samples, as shown by smaller residual df. Complete condition-by-condition flow is deferred to unread SM.
study.design: One dilemma per person. Hunger strike in Experiments 1/2, informal DNR conflict in Experiments 2/3, toxic-gas diversion in Experiment 3. Actual agent decision randomized after a participant recommends one option; response then randomized to normative justification or generic causal-background explanation. Experiment 3 also randomizes human/robot agent and measures trust three times.
study.response_comparison: Justifications cite prioritized norms/values; comparison statements include I had to make a decision and The situation required making a decision. Both communicate intentionality, but normative content and informative specificity differ. This is not a comparison with every possible substantive causal, contrastive or evidence-rich explanation.
study.selection: Free-text blame clarifications are coded to exclude participants disqualifying robot blame or assigning it to a programmer/designer. Authors describe about30% rejecting robots as proper targets; they explicitly limit generalization. Clarification occurs after second blame in Experiment 1, after both in Experiment 2 and after first in Experiment 3, so selection can be post-response in earlier experiments.
study.measurement: Blame 0–100 before/after response. MDMT 10-item parallel short forms, six-point 0–5 plus Does not fit treated missing. Performance mean of four capability/reliability items; moral mean of six sincerity/ethics/benevolence items. Total equals the mean of these two factor scores, available only if both exist, not a simple equal-item average of ten items.
study.moral_disagreement: Divergence between own normative recommendation and randomized actual decision predicts more initial blame; partial eta-squared .22–.40 across seven agent/dilemma combinations, all reported p<.001. These are variations/replications inside three experiments in one article, not seven independent published studies.
study.blame: Response×time mitigation is significant in three of five robot samples and both human samples. Robot hunger-strike Experiment 1 and robot DNR Experiment 2 lack the overall two-way effect but show action-specific three-way interactions, benefiting the inaction path. Do not claim blame falls for every action or all participants.
study.trust: Experiments 1/2 measure trust once after response, showing between-condition total-trust advantages with justification eta-squared 2.4%,2.8%,2.7%. Moral effects 4.9%,1.9%,4.8%; performance .2% nonsignificant,2.5% significant,.4% nonsignificant. No pre-response trust baseline in those two experiments, so these differences alone are not observed recovery.
study.temporal_repair: Experiment 3 baseline→decision→response supports disagreement-associated trust loss and partial recovery in the justification condition relative to generic explanation. Total-trust response×change effects 1.7% robot DNR,5.7% human DNR,4.5% robot toxic gas,3.8% human toxic gas. RobotDNR performance recovery .6% is nonsignificant; moral effects are generally more pronounced but not uniformly larger.
study.normative_scope: Dilemmas deliberately make both options prima facie justifiable. Reduced blame, increased perceived integrity and actual normative correctness are distinct. The study neither resolves resuscitation/hunger-strike clinical obligations nor establishes that robots possess moral feelings, conscience or a lawful mandate.

summary: Add moral justification, trust repair and performance trust, strengthen disagreement/blame/moral-trust evidence and retain measured-trust boundaries. The result concerns short-term perception repair in selected narrative samples, not guaranteed appropriate reliance or proof of ethical decisions.

findings.definition: Offering reasons grounded in norms or values to defend why an action is acceptable or should be chosen.
findings.origin: Moral psychology / reason-giving and human–robot interaction
findings.ai_evidence_status: Randomized normative versus generic-background messages affect human perceptions in narratives; actual ethical warrant, causal faithfulness and live AI behavior remain untested
findings.ai_proposal: Explain a consequential choice by identifying relevant duties, affected interests, competing options, evidence and why the selected priority is warranted. Check that the account matches actual decision rules/actions and can be challenged. Evaluate both valid and misleading justifications; increasing trust must not substitute for correcting an error or respecting consent and authorized scope.
findings.novelty_rationale: A normative defense asks whether reasons warrant an action, not merely what caused it or why it differed from an alternative. It can be sound or unsound, prospective or retrospective, and is not inherently rationalization, an excuse or a license to violate rules for an alleged good end.

evidence.quote: Justifications explicitly refer to normative reasons

findings.evidence_scope: The paper operationalizes justifications as reasons invoking a prioritized norm and compares them with generic causal-history statements in three experiments. Trustworthiness ratings rise and blame sometimes falls, including under disagreement. This demonstrates a conditional communication/perception effect, not that every stated norm is valid or genuinely drove the decision.
findings.boundary: Persuasiveness and moral validity differ. A justification can conceal omissions, misuse a norm or rationalize an unauthorized action. Some actions require correction/remedy rather than a more convincing explanation. A factual account of a model's causal process and a normative defense of its output need separate verification.

findings.definition: Actions intended to restore trust after a failure, violation or disagreement has damaged it.
findings.origin: Relationship and organizational psychology / human–automation interaction
findings.ai_evidence_status: Short-term perceived-trustworthiness repair tested with repeated ratings in one of three narrative experiments; no behavioral reliance, durable relationship repair or actual safety improvement measured
findings.ai_proposal: After an AI failure, distinguish correction of the underlying problem, truthful disclosure, explanation, apology where warranted and effective remedy. Measure whether users' expectations become accurate over time and whether actual performance improves, rather than maximizing restored trust. Test repeated failures and maintain the user's option to stop, withhold reliance or challenge the result.
findings.novelty_rationale: Attempted recovery after a breach differs from initial trust formation or the damage itself. It need not fully succeed, and restored positive ratings are not necessarily warranted or equivalent to renewed behavioral reliance.

evidence.quote: recovering lost trust than the explanation response
we had no behavioral reliance measure

findings.evidence_scope: Experiment 3 measures baseline, post-decision and post-response trustworthiness. Normative messages produce greater partial recovery than generic explanations in the selected samples, especially on moral expectations. Experiments 1/2 have only post-response trust measures and therefore support a between-condition advantage rather than directly observed recovery.
findings.boundary: More trust is not always a desirable repair target: justified distrust should remain until evidence supports renewed reliance. Repairing perceptions does not correct a malfunction, undo harm or establish future competence. A single short hypothetical interaction does not prove long-term recovery or immunity to repeated breaches.

findings.definition: Expecting an agent or system to perform competently and reliably in a relevant task.
findings.origin: Trust research / human factors and human–robot interaction
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit perceived-trustworthiness dimension measured in narratives; observed reliability, actual competence and behavioral dependence are separate and untested
findings.ai_proposal: Assess users' expectations of task capability and consistency separately from beliefs about honesty, benevolence or ethical integrity. Compare those expectations with actual task performance and failure conditions. Test whether a morally appealing explanation creates unjustified capability expectations.
findings.novelty_rationale: Expectations of reliable task performance differ from endorsing values, trusting a source's knowledge or perceiving ability alone. A trustworthy moral rationale need not imply technical capability; performance expectations can change without actual skill changing.

evidence.quote: expectations of trustworthiness as a proxy

findings.evidence_scope: MDMT parallel short forms use four performance items and six moral items, with factor separation/reliability described in unread SM. Normative justification has variable effects on performance scores, including several nulls. The experiment measures perceptions, not actual reliable operation or willingness to accept vulnerability.
findings.boundary: Perceived reliability is not measured reliability. Instrumental performance, information quality and moral integrity can diverge. Capability claims must be task-specific, and subjective scale scores do not authorize delegation or establish that an agent can meet its responsibilities.

findings.definition: Assigning more blame to an advisor whose moral recommendation conflicts with one's own endorsed choice than to an advisor who agrees.
findings.novelty_rationale: Extends the existing disagreement-related blame pattern from advisor recommendations to narrated agents' actual dilemma choices without a duplicate entry.

evidence.quote: decision opposite to the participants’ normative recommendation

findings.evidence_scope: Participants state a normative preference before the agent's randomized decision; disagreement predicts higher initial blame across three dilemmas and both agent types in Experiment 3. Effects concern a selected sample accepting the robot as blameworthy in principle, not every person or every norm conflict.
findings.boundary: A disagreement can reflect valid reasons to criticize, not merely an irrational penalty. Normative preference is measured rather than randomized, and differing action meanings/convictions remain relevant. Partial recovery after reasons does not prove people abandoned their original moral position.

findings.definition: Willingness to endorse the values or ethical commitments one attributes to an advisor.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds an explicitly different moral-trust operationalization based on perceived sincerity, ethical integrity and benevolence rather than silently equating it with values endorsement.

evidence.quote: Moral trust (i.e., ethical integrity, transparency, benevolence)

findings.evidence_scope: The MDMT moral factor asks about attributed moral qualities, with several effects stronger than performance expectations. This overlaps with but is not the same measure as endorsement of an advisor's commitments in earlier evidence. It is not proof of actual conscience, agreement with every decision or verified integrity.
findings.boundary: Retain distinctions among endorsed values, perceived moral trustworthiness, felt vulnerability and behavioral reliance. A source's broader moral-trust label does not automatically make all these constructs interchangeable or justify changing the existing definition without a dedicated ontology reconciliation.

findings.definition: A reduction in trust following a failure, which can remain after that failure is reported corrected.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds repeated perceived-trustworthiness measures following a moral disagreement, distinct from an observed technical malfunction or a uniform permanent loss.
findings.evidence_scope: Experiment 3 measures decline after the narrated decision, especially when it conflicts with a participant's prior recommendation. No underlying device failure is repaired; justification can partially recover perceived trustworthiness without returning all dimensions to baseline.
findings.boundary: Disagreement and technical failure can produce different trust trajectories. A decline may be justified, and recovery need not imply changed performance. Separate perceived reliability, integrity and actual reliance over repeated interactions.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds explicit deserved-blame ratings and response-dependent change, unlike the earlier mixed fault/causation index.

evidence.quote: How much blame does the [agent] deserve

findings.evidence_scope: Two 0–100 deserved-blame judgments are collected before/after an assigned response. Justifications reduce blame overall in some samples and only for one action in others. Participants who reject robots as blame targets are excluded, a substantive scope restriction rather than evidence all humans blame robots.
findings.boundary: Moral criticism, causal responsibility and legal accountability differ. Excluding institutional-blame interpretations does not invalidate those interpretations; it narrows the research population. Reduced blame is not proof the action was permissible or that actual harm was remedied.

findings.definition: Using assistance to a degree justified by its task-specific competence, relevance, uncertainty and the consequences of error.
findings.novelty_rationale: Separates successful perception repair from appropriate behavioral use, which the authors explicitly say remains unmeasured.

evidence.quote: we had no behavioral reliance measure

findings.evidence_scope: No delegation, error detection, willingness-to-risk behavior or task outcome establishes calibration. Boundary-only evidence, excluded from direct reliance paper coverage.
findings.boundary: A normative explanation can increase confidence without improving capability. Evaluate truthfulness, actual decision warrant and reliance separately; do not optimize trust repair to conceal justified objections.

methodological_limits: Narratives about future robots, one dilemma per participant and US-registered online adults limit ecological and cultural generalization. No live robot, implemented justification generator, actual care decision or repeated long-term relationship was tested.

Reported N=3,596 sums the experiment datasets, not every complete-case analytic sample. Denominator df and missing-factor rules show smaller samples. Full exclusions/attrition and which initial Ns include which filtering stages require the unread SM; do not label all 3,596 as analyzed for every outcome.

Approximately 30% reject robot blame or shift responsibility to designers. This is a meaningful philosophical/population subgroup, not necessarily inattention. Excluding it narrows generalization, can differ by agent type and may affect treatment estimates because coding occurs after response in Experiments 1/2. Preregistration does not remove this selection limitation.

Does not fit trust responses are treated as missing. People rejecting robot moral attributes may therefore be systematically absent from trust factors. Available-case Ns differ across total, moral and performance scores, and total requires both subscales.

Trust is expressly a proxy: perceived trustworthiness rather than a separately measured state of vulnerability or actual behavioral reliance. The source distinguishes these constructs; summary claims must retain that distinction.

Generic explanation controls are close to procedural/tautological statements. They do not match substantive causal evidence, meaningful contrastive reasons, information quantity or a transparent trace. The result is relative to these controls, not proof only moral justifications can repair trust.

There is no silent/no-response comparator. Difference between explanation and justification does not establish all explanations have zero effect, all normative reasons are valid or justifications are necessary for every repair.

Selected justifications come from frequent pretest reasons; popularity is not ethical truth. Dilemmas were designed with both paths prima facie justifiable. Strong convictions, actual rights, medical rules or unjustifiable conduct may produce different effects.

Actual agent decisions and responses are randomized, supporting conditional effects of the narrative manipulations. Participants' prior recommendations, perceived moral priorities and acceptance of robot agency are measured; the design does not uniquely identify a moral-integrity mechanism.

Experiments 1/2 have one trust measurement after response; only Experiment 3 observes baseline loss and recovery. Some dimensions remain below baseline, and not every robot performance-recovery effect is significant. Recovery means partial change, not full restoration or stable future trust.

Blame mitigation has action-specific nulls. In two robot samples the overall response×time test is null while the action-dependent three-way test is significant. Do not compress these into a universal reduction for either available decision.

Moral and performance factors are correlated and use different items. Two significant versus nonsignificant effects do not by themselves establish their difference. ANCOVA controlling one post-response trust factor for another is not a causal separation; the hunger-strike Experiment 2 moral effect becomes nonsignificant after performance adjustment.

Parallel short forms and reliability/factor checks are reported, with detailed loadings in unread SM. Internal consistency and factor structure do not establish true morality, actual capability or measurement invariance for every human/robot subgroup.

Skewed blame/trust distributions are analyzed with ANOVAs; transformed/subset robustness is asserted in SM but not independently checked here. The broad claim that no nonparametric alternatives exist is not endorsed; full design/data would be needed for a separate statistical review.

Table 3 first row pairs p=.86 with partial eta-squared 0.3% for an F(1,339) test. A p=.86 F corresponds to about .0092%, whereas .3% implies F≈1.02. This visible numeric mismatch needs fitted-output verification and does not turn that null overall effect into a positive result.

Effect sizes shown as percentages are partial variance proportions, not percent increases in trust, percent people convinced or probabilities of safety. Multiple factors, dilemmas, outcomes and tests are reported; full preregistered decisions/multiplicity plan were not inspected.

A prioritization defense is not necessarily faithful to an agent's real causal process. Study messages are assigned narrative statements, not verified actual machine intentions or traces. No evidence shows the robot really cares, chooses norms autonomously or possesses sincerity as an inner state.

The elaboration-likelihood explanation and possible central-route durable persuasion are explicitly speculative. No central/peripheral processing intervention or long-term attitude measurement is provided.

The no-reachable-supervisor medical and toxic-gas dilemmas force binary options for research. Real institutions may have additional alternatives, binding clinical rules and required escalation. The source is not a clinical, legal or system-deployment recommendation.

Three experiments, seven agent/dilemma cells and a cited 2023 preprint do not provide eleven independent papers. Preprint/final data overlap requires direct comparison before counting an independent replication; no automatic duplicate-study credit is assigned.

source_corrections.problem: Caption says parenthetical letters identify panels in Figure 2.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: They correspond to Figure 3: robot DNR(a), human DNR(b), Experiment 2 hunger-strike(c). Figure 2 shows disagreement crossovers rather than these mitigation panels.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Direct table/figure inspection; no external correction inferred.

source_corrections.problem: Both repeat Malle and Ullman's 2021 multidimensional human–robot trust chapter, pages 3–25.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Treat as one bibliographic work, not two independent sources. The original book chapter was not fully read here.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Exact duplicate title/authors/book/locator comparison within supplied references.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Moral trust can mean endorsing an advisor's values or attributing integrity/benevolence; these operationalizations overlap without being identical. Moral rebound after conflicting advice differs from repairing trust after a norm conflict.

The existing moral-disagreement penalty extends to actual narrated choices. More blame under disagreement and persisting respect after a justification can coexist; neither implies people changed their initial moral preference.

Valuing explanations or being persuaded by a reason is not demonstrated oversight use. Real-time workload and available authority can prevent even a clear justification from supporting successful intervention.

Perceived trustworthiness, confidence, acceptance and calibrated reliance are separate. This paper provides the perception time course but explicitly lacks the behavior/error-detection evidence called for by the conceptual reliance framework.

Blameworthiness is measured directly here rather than combined with a causal-contribution item. Both papers still require separation of descriptive blame from legal duty, actual control and ethical correctness.

deferred.reason: Capacity and decision-context constructs central to the theoretical setup, not newly verified capabilities of a deployed robot. Retain under the justification and uncertainty boundaries rather than infer actual machine morality.
A specific conditional effect already represented by moral justification and blame-attribution evidence. Avoid another near-duplicate effect entry when some action paths are null.
Explicit speculation based on secondary persuasion theory. No processing-path or long-term test is performed.
Earlier cited studies are not fully read here. The present experiment does not ask an actual robot to refuse an unsafe command; do not import those outcomes as new direct evidence.
Similar descriptive patterns are not a formal equivalence result, universal generalization or equal moral/legal status. Selection excludes important robot-skeptical respondents.

limitations: Three communicative/relational/perception concepts added; existing entries strengthened with selected-sample scope and relevant nulls. No moral correctness, restored actual performance, behavioral calibration or universal superiority of justifications is claimed; no automatic normative links added.
